book.title: Talk
book.subtitle: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves
book.edition: First US hardcover, Crown, January 21, 2025 (ISBN 9780593443491); ebook January 21, 2025 (ISBN 9780593443507); US paperback January 27, 2026 (ISBN 9780593443514); audiobook read by the author, 10 hours 1 minute (ISBN 9780593446096). 336 pages per the publisher and Google Books. UK edition published by Penguin.
book.author_credibility: Alison Wood Brooks is the O'Brien Associate Professor of Business Administration and a Hellman Faculty Fellow at Harvard Business School, where she created and teaches an MBA course called TALK; she has published widely in top psychology and management journals on question-asking, humor, topic selection, apologies, and anxiety. The book draws heavily on her own lab's studies, so the author is promoting her own research program. Several of her papers were coauthored with Francesca Gino, whose work was found to contain data problems. The Many Co-Authors project lists the Gino-coauthored papers relevant here (Huang et al. 2017; Yeomans et al. 2020; Collins et al. 2022); in coauthor-submitted (unvetted) responses, none of their studies is attributed to Gino as data handler, and no misconduct finding against these papers or against Brooks was located. Readers may still weight Gino-coauthored findings cautiously.
book.evidence_base: Mostly peer-reviewed experimental and field research (lab conversations, speed dates, sales calls, parole hearings, traffic stops, transcripts analyzed with natural language processing), from Brooks's lab and others (Epley, Mastroianni, Minson, Schweitzer, Aron). Supplemented by classroom exercises, observations, and anecdotes. Some topic-selection findings (topic preparation, topic prediction, topic switching) come from Brooks and Yeomans work for which no peer-reviewed article was located.

legal_access.note: Publisher page read: description, TALK maxims, formats, ISBNs, 336 pages, Look Inside sample

Free 22-page TALK workbook by the author (Crown 2025); read in full. Confirms TALK maxims, conversational compass, topic pyramid, topic prep, receptiveness recipe, compliments, apologies, and book sections on Difficult Moments, Groups, and Apologies
Greater Good article by Kira M. Newman summarizing ten findings from the book (not an adaptation by Brooks); read in full
LIFTOFF podcast (host Ilana Gilovich) with Brooks on the topic pyramid; transcript read
LIFTOFF podcast episode on endings with Brooks and Adam Mastroianni; transcript read
Author interview on the TALK maxims; not re-read in verification
Google Books record (336 pages); preview search was rate-limited

insights.name: The TALK maxims
insights.explanation: Brooks organizes conversational skill into four maxims: Topics (choose good topics and manage them well), Asking (ask more, and better, questions), Levity (use humor and warmth to keep the exchange lively), and Kindness (try to prioritize your partner's conversational needs). She frames conversation as a coordination game that is harder than it looks, and the maxims as short reminders of where it usually goes wrong, so you can diagnose a stalled exchange and pick the right fix. They are a checklist, not a script.
insights.when_to_use: Before an important conversation to plan, and afterwards to debrief what worked and what stalled.
insights.worked_example: After a flat one-on-one with a new direct report, a manager runs the four letters: Topics, we only covered ticket status; Asking, I asked two questions, both yes or no; Levity, nobody laughed once; Kindness, I talked 70 percent of the time. Next week she brings two non-status topics, plans one open follow-up, and deliberately lets the report lead the first ten minutes.
common_mistakes: Treating TALK as a script to recite rather than a diagnostic lens
Working on only one letter (usually Asking) and ignoring the rest
Forcing humor or depth when the partner's needs call for something else
steps: Before: list a few topics you could raise and one or two open questions
During: notice which letter is failing (stale topic, no questions, no lightness, one-sided)
Adjust: switch topic, ask a follow-up, add a light remark, or hand the floor back
After: rate each letter briefly and pick one to improve next time
situations: Debriefing a conversation that felt awkward
Preparing for a first meeting with a new manager
Improving weekly one-on-ones
Reconnecting with a friend you have drifted from

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), overall structure: opening framing of conversation as a coordination game, then one part per TALK maxim, followed by material on difficult moments, groups, and apologies (per the author's TALK workbook); exact chapter titles not verified
source.underlying_research: Synthesis of Brooks's conversation research program at Harvard Business School (speed dates, sales calls, parole hearings, structured lab chats) plus wider literature

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the publisher description and the author's workbook. The acronym is an organizing device by a credible conversation researcher; the components draw on peer-reviewed work of varying strength, but the framework as a whole has not been tested as a unit.

insights.name: Prepare topics in advance
insights.explanation: Most people walk into conversations expecting topics to arrive on their own, and feel that preparing them would be awkward or calculating. Brooks reports that only a small minority (about 18 percent) prepare topics, and about half think doing so would make the conversation less enjoyable. Yet in her research even about thirty seconds of planning made conversations flow better, with fewer awkward pauses and filler words, and left people less anxious and more confident; her MBA students, who resist the exercise, reliably enjoy prepared-topic conversations more. You do not have to raise every item: the list is insurance for a lull and a nudge toward richer subjects than whatever comes to mind first. People are also poor at predicting which topics will turn out well, so several options beat betting on one.
insights.when_to_use: Networking events, first dates, dinners with in-laws, client lunches, skip-level meetings, any situation where you fear dead air.
insights.worked_example: Heading to a client dinner, an account lead writes four possible topics in her phone: the client's recent office move, a book she knows the client posted about, a light question about weekend plans, and one industry trend she is curious about. When the conversation stalls after the menu, she pulls the office move topic, which turns into a twenty-minute exchange about remote work.
common_mistakes: Rigidly working through the list instead of following the partner's energy
Preparing only safe, generic topics (weather, traffic)
Preparing monologues rather than topics that invite the other person in
Assuming you can tell in advance which topic will land
steps: Take about thirty seconds before the conversation to write down around five possible topics
Mix light and more substantive options, and include something about the other person
Keep the list handy (phone or calendar note) but out of sight
Use it when a lull hits; drop it when the conversation has its own momentum
situations: Attending a networking event alone
First date
Client lunch or dinner
Holiday gathering with relatives you rarely see
Coffee chat with a senior leader

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), T (Topics) maxim; workbook exercise 'Prep topics'
source.underlying_research: Brooks and colleagues' topic-preparation studies (about 18 percent prepare; brief planning reduced pauses and anxiety) and Yeomans and Brooks topic-prediction study (about 1,000 people rated 50 topics, then discussed them; enjoyment was poorly predicted), as reported from the book by Greater Good; no peer-reviewed article located. Plus Brooks's classroom observations.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book via the Greater Good summary and the author's workbook. Rests on Brooks's own studies with Yeomans, which I could not find as peer-reviewed publications, plus teaching experience. Plausible and low-cost; Medium retained.

insights.name: The topic pyramid: climb from small talk, and switch before it goes stale
insights.explanation: Brooks pictures topics as a pyramid with three tiers: small talk at the base (topics any group could discuss), tailored talk in the middle (topics personalized to the people present), and deep talk at the top (topics only this particular group could have). Small talk is not the problem; it is an unavoidable ritual and a treasure hunt for something better. The common mistake is staying on base-level topics, or any spent topic, too long. Signs a topic is running dry include uncomfortable laughter, longer mutual pauses, and repeated statements. When you notice them, either climb (usually with a follow-up question on something that sparked interest) or switch assertively to a new topic; you can call back to earlier topics later. In her studies, pairs asked to cover more topics enjoyed the conversation more without losing depth, and more people felt they had covered too few topics than too many. Not every conversation needs to reach the top.
insights.when_to_use: Whenever a conversation is polite but flat, or when you notice the same points being repeated.
insights.worked_example: At a school pickup, two parents have covered the weather and the bake sale twice. One says, 'That bake sale saga has had a good run. Can I ask, how are you finding the new job you mentioned last month?' The switch acknowledges the old topic and moves to something more personal, and the chat comes alive.
common_mistakes: Abandoning a topic abruptly without acknowledging it
Jumping straight to intense personal questions with someone you just met
Staying on a dying topic out of politeness
Assuming every conversation should end up deep
steps: Notice signals that a topic is spent: uncomfortable laughter, longer mutual pauses, repetition
When something sparks interest, climb with a follow-up question toward tailored talk
Otherwise switch assertively to a fresh topic, briefly affirming the old one if it helps
Call back to earlier topics that deserved more airtime, and match depth to the relationship
situations: Small talk that keeps circling
Team lunch with colleagues you barely know
Catching up with an old friend
Long car ride with a partner

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), T (Topics) maxim; workbook exercises 'Be a topic leader' and 'Stick with small talk'; LIFTOFF podcast episode 4 interview
source.underlying_research: Brooks and colleagues' topic-switching studies as reported from the book: strangers asked to cover 12 topics in 10 minutes rated enjoyment higher (about 5 to 6 on a 7-point scale) than those talking normally; in 30-minute online chats, 20 percent felt they covered too few topics versus 11 percent too many. Yeomans seminar abstract reports people are poor at detecting whether a partner wants to stay on or switch. No peer-reviewed article located.

insights.confidence_rationale: Pyramid and switching advice confirmed in the author's workbook, podcast interview, and Greater Good summary of the book. The pyramid is a teaching metaphor and the switching evidence comes from Brooks lab studies not located in peer-reviewed form, so specific switching claims are provisional.

insights.name: Ask more questions, especially follow-ups
insights.explanation: People ask fewer questions than would serve them, overestimate how many they ask, and do not expect questions to make them more liked. In live online chats, people instructed to ask more questions were liked more, an effect the authors attribute largely to follow-up questions, the ones that build on what the other person just said, because they signal listening and care (responsiveness). Brooks also reports that in speed dates, people who asked more follow-ups got more second dates and nobody reached a point of asking too many.
insights.when_to_use: First meetings, interviews (on either side), one-on-ones, dates, and catching up with family; any time you want the other person to feel heard.
insights.worked_example: A colleague mentions she spent the weekend helping her father move. Instead of saying 'Nice, I went hiking,' you ask, 'How did he feel about leaving the old place?' Her answer leads to a real conversation about aging parents, and later that week she seeks you out for advice on a project.
common_mistakes: Asking a rapid-fire list of unrelated questions that feels like an interrogation
Asking a question only as a lead-in to your own story
Stacking several questions at once so the person cannot answer any well
Asking follow-ups without actually listening to the answer
steps: Listen for a detail, feeling, or surprise in what the person just said
Ask one open question about that detail (how, what was it like, what happened next)
Let them answer fully before sharing your own related experience
Balance: share about yourself too, so it stays reciprocal
situations: First conversation with a new teammate
Job interview, as candidate or interviewer
Speed networking
Catching up with a teenager after school
First date

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), A (Asking) maxim; Brooks and Leslie K. John, 'The Surprising Power of Questions,' Harvard Business Review 96(3), May-June 2018
source.underlying_research: Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson and Gino (2017), 'It Doesn't Hurt to Ask: Question-Asking Increases Liking,' Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 113(3), 430-452 (two chat experiments with modest effects, plus speed-dating field data). Critique: Kluger and Malloy (2019), 'Question Asking as a Dyadic Behavior,' JPSP 117(6), 1127-1138, found the speed-dating association vanished once actor and partner effects were controlled. Integrity note: Gino-coauthored; listed by the Many Co-Authors project, where coauthor responses attribute none of its studies to Gino as data handler.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book via the Greater Good summary and the workbook. The experimental effects are real but modest (d about 0.3), and Kluger and Malloy's reanalysis argues the speed-dating link to second dates does not survive proper controls and that follow-up and switch questions were hard to separate. Gino coauthorship noted per user decision; the audit project shows no Gino-handled studies. Medium and 'contested' retained.

insights.name: Four kinds of questions
insights.explanation: Brooks and John sort conversational questions into four types: introductory (opening, such as 'How are you?'), mirror (returning the same question, such as 'Good, and you?'), full-switch (changing the subject entirely), and follow-up (asking more about what was just said). Each has a use, but follow-ups are the most underused and the most valuable for connection. Mirror and switch questions are fine in moderation; too many switches can feel like a checklist. Open-ended phrasing and attention to sequence and tone also matter.
insights.when_to_use: When you want to audit your own question habits, or plan questions for an interview, discovery call, or check-in.
insights.worked_example: Reviewing notes from a sales discovery call, a rep notices most of his questions were full-switch ('Next, what is your budget? And your timeline?'). On the next call he deliberately asks a follow-up after each answer ('You said the last vendor was slow to respond; what did that cost you?') and learns the real buying criterion.
common_mistakes: Using only introductory and mirror questions and never getting past pleasantries
Treating a question list as a sequence to march through
Asking closed yes or no questions when you want depth
steps: Open with an introductory question
After each answer, default to one follow-up before switching
Use full-switch questions deliberately when a topic is exhausted
Prefer open phrasing (what, how, tell me about) for depth
situations: Sales discovery call
Interviewing a job candidate
Stakeholder interview for a project
Check-in with a struggling teammate

source.citation: Brooks and John, 'The Surprising Power of Questions,' Harvard Business Review, May-June 2018 (taxonomy read on hbr.org); related material in Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), A (Asking) maxim
source.underlying_research: Huang et al. (2017) JPSP 113(3), 430-452; taxonomy developed from human coding and machine learning of conversation transcripts

insights.confidence_rationale: Taxonomy confirmed in the author's HBR article; the workbook confirms the book's emphasis on balancing follow-up and topic-switching questions, though I could not see the full four-type list in the book itself. It is a descriptive tool rather than a tested intervention, and the claim that follow-ups matter most rests on the evidence (and critique) noted for insight 04.

insights.name: Do not boomerask
insights.explanation: Boomerasking is asking someone a question, letting them answer, and then answering it yourself instead of following up on what they said: 'How was your weekend?' followed by a long account of yours. Brooks and Yeomans identify three variants: ask-bragging, ask-complaining, and ask-sharing. Boomeraskers believe they come across well, but partners see them as insincere, self-focused, and uninterested, and prefer people who simply disclose directly. If you want to share, share; if you ask, stay with their answer.
insights.when_to_use: Anytime you notice yourself asking a question you are itching to answer, especially at social events and in team check-ins.
insights.worked_example: On Monday standup a teammate asks, 'Did anyone catch the game?' and then talks for three minutes about his own reaction. A better version: he says, 'I watched the game last night and loved the finish. Did you see it?' and then listens to what others thought. Personally, the same applies when asking a partner about their day only to pivot to your own frustrations.
common_mistakes: Using a question as a launch pad for your own story
Asking and then half-listening while you wait to speak
Thinking that announcing your news via a question is more modest or polite
Ask-complaining: asking about their week so you can vent about yours
steps: Before asking, check: do I want their answer, or a cue to talk?
If you want to share, just share, then invite their view
If you asked, follow up on their answer at least once before bringing in your own
situations: Monday check-in with the team
Dinner party conversation
Asking a partner about their day
Reconnecting at a reunion

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), A (Asking) maxim (reported in the Greater Good summary of the book)
source.underlying_research: Brooks and Yeomans (2025), 'Boomerasking: Answering Your Own Questions,' Journal of Experimental Psychology: General 154(3), 864-893 (eight studies)

insights.confidence_rationale: Abstract read: multi-study paper in a top journal, but from the author's own team and recent, so not yet independently replicated. The first-pass claim that boomerasking makes partners like the topic less was not found in the abstract and was removed.

insights.name: Sensitive questions cost less than you fear
insights.explanation: People avoid personal or sensitive questions (about money, health, relationships, setbacks) because they expect the other person to feel uncomfortable and think less of them. Research Brooks cites finds askers overestimate these costs: being asked sensitive questions did not make conversations less enjoyable or create worse impressions of the asker than mundane questions did. How you ask still matters, so phrasing with care, giving an easy out, and asking in private help. Her workbook suggests rehearsing hard questions with a trusted partner.
insights.when_to_use: When you need information that feels awkward to request, or when a relationship would benefit from going past surface topics.
insights.worked_example: A team lead suspects a strong performer is quietly job hunting. Rather than guessing, she asks privately, 'I want to make sure you are getting what you need here. Are you thinking about other opportunities?' He is relieved to talk, and they agree on a stretch project. At home, the same principle helps a sibling finally ask a parent how their finances are holding up.
common_mistakes: Asking a sensitive question in front of others
Leading with judgment or assumptions inside the question
Never asking because the fear feels convincing
Pressing after the person signals they do not want to answer
steps: Notice when you are avoiding a question purely from fear of awkwardness
Choose a private moment
Frame the purpose (why you are asking) and keep wording neutral
Make it easy to decline, then listen without judgment
situations: Asking a report whether they are thinking of leaving
Discussing salary with a peer
Asking an aging parent about finances or health
Asking a friend how they are really coping after a loss

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), A (Asking) maxim (reported in the Greater Good summary of the book); workbook exercise 'Asking and answering hard questions'
source.underlying_research: Hart, VanEpps and Schweitzer (2021), 'The (better than expected) consequences of asking sensitive questions,' Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 162, 136-154 (corrigendum in OBHDP 165, 250); five experiments

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed as cited in the book via the Greater Good summary (which links this paper). Five experiments in one paper, consistent with broader findings that people overestimate social awkwardness. Still one paper, mostly with strangers; workplace power differences may change the calculus. Removed the unverified 'preregistered' and sample-size details.

insights.name: Levity: lightness over jokes
insights.explanation: Brooks treats boredom as a quiet killer of conversation and levity as the fix. Levity is broader than telling jokes: humor, warmth, laughing at others' humor, playful asides, and callbacks (references to something said earlier in the conversation or the relationship) all keep a conversation lively. When her students recorded talks with their favorite conversation partner, nearly all of those partners used callbacks. People underestimate how often humor attempts go well; successful humor can raise perceived competence and status, while failed or inappropriate humor lowers it, so low-risk levity is usually the better bet than ambitious jokes.
insights.when_to_use: Long meetings, tense negotiations at a safe moment, first meetings, family gatherings that are dragging.
insights.worked_example: Forty minutes into a budget review, a director refers back to a colleague's earlier quip about the 'haunted spreadsheet' when the same file errors again. The room laughs, energy lifts, and the group finishes the remaining items faster. She avoids jokes at anyone's expense and lets others' humor take center stage.
common_mistakes: Believing you must be naturally funny to bring levity
Telling edgy or inappropriate jokes, which can lower status
Using humor to dodge a serious concern the other person raised
Joking at someone else's expense
steps: Notice when energy is dropping
Reach for low-risk levity: laugh at others' humor, a light callback, a playful aside, or thanks
Keep humor inclusive and on-topic
Read the room and drop it quickly if it does not land
situations: Long or tense team meeting
Opening a negotiation
Family dinner that has gone quiet
Onboarding a new hire

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), L (Levity) maxim; workbook exercises 'Escalate' and 'Levity reframe'; author interviews (Think Fast Talk Smart episode 223 with Naomi Bagdonas)
source.underlying_research: Bitterly, Brooks and Schweitzer (2017), 'Risky Business: When Humor Increases and Decreases Status,' Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 112(3), 431-455; Brooks's classroom recordings of students' favorite conversation partners (callbacks)

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the book via the Greater Good summary and workbook. The humor and status finding comes from a multi-experiment JPSP paper by the author's team; the callback observation is classroom evidence, and the broader claim that levity combats boredom is credible expert synthesis.

insights.name: Kindness as receptiveness in disagreement
insights.explanation: For Brooks, kindness in conversation means trying to prioritize your partner's conversational needs, which includes being visibly open to views you disagree with. Her receptiveness recipe: acknowledge the other view, affirm and validate their feelings, hedge your claims, avoid argumentative explanation words such as 'because' and 'therefore', frame things positively, and even voice your own internal disagreement. Two misperceptions make conflict worse: we tend to judge people who disagree with us as poor listeners even when they listened well, and if you assume the other person is out to persuade you rather than learn from you, you behave in ways that escalate. Shifting your aim from winning to learning tends, ironically, to make you more persuasive.
insights.when_to_use: Disagreements at work, political or values conversations with family, feedback discussions, contentious online threads.
insights.worked_example: In a design review, an engineer disagrees with a product manager's launch date. Instead of 'That date is impossible,' she says, 'I understand the market window matters, and I agree we need to ship this quarter. My worry is the testing time; it might be that a two-week slip saves us a rollback.' The PM engages with the risk rather than defending the date.
common_mistakes: Faking agreement or hedging so much the point disappears
Acknowledging the other view in a sarcastic tone
Assuming the other person is purely trying to persuade or win
Treating kindness as niceness rather than responsiveness
steps: Acknowledge: restate the other person's view in a sentence
Affirm and validate: name a point of agreement or the sense in how they feel
Hedge: soften absolutes (might, in my experience) and skip 'because' and 'therefore' lecturing
Reframe to the positive: state what you want, not only what you oppose
Assume they are trying to learn too, and aim to learn rather than win
situations: Pushing back on a deadline in a meeting
Talking politics with a relative
Replying to a heated email or Slack thread
Disagreeing with a partner about money

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), K (Kindness) maxim and material on difficult moments; workbook exercise 'De-escalate' (receptiveness recipe); Greater Good summary of the book
source.underlying_research: Yeomans, Minson, Collins, Chen and Gino (2020), 'Conversational receptiveness: Improving engagement with opposing views,' OBHDP 160, 131-148; Collins, Dorison, Gino and Minson (2022), 'Underestimating Counterparts' Learning Goals Impairs Conflictual Conversations,' Psychological Science 33(10), 1732-1752; Ren and Schaumberg (2024), 'Disagreement Gets Mistaken for Bad Listening,' Psychological Science 35(5), 455-470. The related HEAR acronym (Hedge, Emphasize agreement, Acknowledge, Reframe) comes from Minson and Yeomans's teaching and was not found in Brooks's materials. Integrity note: the 2020 and 2022 papers are Gino-coauthored; the Many Co-Authors project lists both, with coauthor responses attributing none of their studies to Gino as data handler.

insights.confidence_rationale: Book's version (receptiveness recipe) confirmed in the author's workbook; the disagreement-listening and learning-goals findings confirmed via the Greater Good summary. Multi-study peer-reviewed work including field data, consistent with negotiation research. Gino coauthorship noted per user decision. Medium retained.

insights.name: Give the compliment and the thanks you are holding back
insights.explanation: People underestimate how good a sincere compliment or expression of thanks will make the other person feel, and overestimate how awkward it will be, so they give fewer than they should. Brooks recommends complimenting things you genuinely admire, especially choices and efforts, and steering clear of remarks about physical appearance unless you know they are welcome. Do not worry about perfect wording; the warmth is what lands.
insights.when_to_use: After a colleague does good work, when a friend helps you, when a family member's effort goes unnoticed, in written notes or messages.
insights.worked_example: A project manager notices a junior analyst rebuilt a messy dashboard overnight. She sends a two-line message: 'The way you restructured the filters made the exec review so much smoother. Thank you for taking that on.' The analyst later says it was the most motivating note she had received that year. At home, the same manager thanks her partner specifically for handling the school forms she had been dreading.
common_mistakes: Waiting for the perfect phrasing and never sending it
Giving vague praise ('great job') instead of naming what was good
Complimenting appearance in professional or uncertain settings
Using compliments as a set-up for a request
steps: Notice a specific action, choice, or quality you admire
Say or write it plainly, naming the effect it had
Skip the over-explanation and accept that it may feel awkward to you, not them
situations: Recognizing a teammate's extra effort
Thank-you note to a mentor
Appreciating a partner's invisible work
Congratulating a friend on a milestone

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), K (Kindness) maxim (compliment guidance reported in the Greater Good summary); workbook exercises 'Give a compliment' and 'Battle of the nice guys'
source.underlying_research: Zhao and Epley (2021), 'Insufficiently complimentary?: Underestimating the positive impact of compliments creates a barrier to expressing them,' Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 121(2), 239-256 (confirmed as cited via Greater Good). Kumar and Epley (2018), 'Undervaluing Gratitude: Expressers Misunderstand the Consequences of Showing Appreciation,' Psychological Science 29(9), 1423-1435 (supports the thanks part; not confirmed as cited in the book).

insights.confidence_rationale: Compliment advice confirmed in the book via the Greater Good summary and workbook. The miscalibration appears across multiple experiments in two separate papers and fits a broader set of social-underestimation findings, so High retained; the gratitude paper is not confirmed as cited, and the advice about avoiding appearance comments is the author's guidance rather than a tested result.

insights.name: End before the well runs dry
insights.explanation: Conversations rarely end when both people want them to: in a study of 932 conversations, very few ended when both wanted, or even when one wanted, and people were poor at guessing when their partner wanted to stop. Brooks treats the ending as the final coordination problem of a conversation and, in interviews, says most of us stay too long, just as we do on topics. She finds this freeing: getting the end exactly right is hard for everyone, and a good conversation ending is not the end of the relationship but one in a sequence of conversations. Practical implication: watch for fading energy and close warmly rather than dragging on.
insights.when_to_use: Networking chats, phone calls with relatives, meetings that have covered the agenda, dates.
insights.worked_example: At a conference reception, a consultant senses a conversation with a prospective client winding down after a good exchange about supply chains. She says, 'This has been the best conversation of my night. I will send you that article on nearshoring tomorrow,' and moves on. The prospect replies to the follow-up email the next morning.
common_mistakes: Staying because you assume the other person wants to continue
Leaving abruptly without a warm close
Over-apologizing for ending
Letting meetings run to the full slot when the work is done
steps: Notice fading energy: repetition, shorter turns, glances away
Signal the close with appreciation or a callback
Name a next step if there is one
Exit cleanly
situations: Leaving a conversation at a networking event
Ending a long call with a parent
Wrapping a meeting early
Ending a first date on a good note

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025) (discusses the Mastroianni et al. study, per the Greater Good summary); Brooks interview on LIFTOFF podcast episode 9 'When it's time to end'
source.underlying_research: Mastroianni, Gilbert, Cooney and Wilson (2021), 'Do conversations end when people want them to?' PNAS 118(10), e2011809118 (932 conversations, intimate partners and strangers)

insights.confidence_rationale: The book cites the Mastroianni study, and Brooks's view that we tend to stay too long is confirmed in her own interview; specific closing tactics (callback, next step) are general guidance not confirmed in the book. The mismatch finding is one well-powered PNAS paper by another lab; the advice is a reasonable inference, not directly tested.

insights.name: The conversational compass: plot your goals and your partner's
insights.explanation: Brooks maps what people want from a conversation on two axes: informational (is the goal about accurate information exchange or not) and relational (is it in service of the partner and relationship, or of yourself). The four quadrants are labeled Advance (high informational, low relational, such as persuading or deciding), Connect (high on both, such as brainstorming or being honest), Protect (low on both, such as concealing or assigning blame), and Savor (high relational, low informational, such as reminiscing or having fun). Unlike many two-by-two models, the aim is not to live in one quadrant; everyone always has at least one goal and usually several, often in different quadrants, and they can conflict. Plotting your goals and your best guess at your partner's makes your choices more intentional.
insights.when_to_use: Before negotiations, feedback conversations, and any talk where you feel torn between getting answers and keeping things pleasant.
insights.worked_example: Before a salary conversation, an employee writes: my information goal is to learn the band and what would justify the top; my relationship goal is to keep my manager as an ally. That leads her to ask open questions about criteria first, rather than opening with a demand that could make the manager defensive.
common_mistakes: Assuming your partner shares your main goal
Sacrificing the relationship for a single piece of information
Being so pleasant that the needed information never surfaces
steps: Before the conversation, list your goals and place each on the compass
Do the same for your best guess of your partner's goals
Note shared and conflicting goals and decide which matter most
Afterward, check which goals were met and whether they shifted
situations: Asking for a raise
Giving critical feedback to a friend who is also a colleague
Vendor negotiation
Hard conversation with a teenager

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025) (conversational compass); workbook exercises 'Plot your goals ahead of time' and 'Plot your goals after'
source.underlying_research: Yeomans, Schweitzer and Brooks (2022), 'The Conversational Circumplex: Identifying, prioritizing, and pursuing informational and relational motives in conversation,' Current Opinion in Psychology 44, 293-302

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the author's workbook, which presents the compass and quadrants from the book. It is a theoretical review framework from credible researchers, not a tested intervention.

insights.name: Apologize, even for what is not your fault
insights.explanation: Brooks treats apologies as a core conversational skill. A sincere apology for a real mistake means saying you are sorry, committing to change, and then following through; she notes that taking responsibility tends to help rather than hurt (for example, physicians who apologize to patients are reported to be sued less). A smaller, surprising finding from her own research: superfluous apologies, expressions of regret for something you clearly did not cause (the rain, the traffic), signal empathic concern and increase trust. In a field study, a stranger who opened with an apology for the rain before asking to borrow a phone got far more yeses than one who simply asked.
insights.when_to_use: After you have let someone down, before asking a stranger or busy colleague for a favor, when someone is dealing with bad luck or a frustrating circumstance.
insights.worked_example: A project lead missed a client deadline because she underestimated testing time. On the call she says, 'I am sorry we missed Friday. I underestimated testing, and that is on me. From now on I will add a buffer and flag risk a week out,' then does so on the next milestone. Separately, when a visiting client arrives soaked, she opens with 'I am so sorry about this weather' before getting started, a small signal that she cares about their experience.
common_mistakes: Apologizing without any commitment to change, or not following through
Hedged non-apologies ('sorry if you were offended')
Over-apologizing until it sounds like low confidence
Avoiding an apology out of fear it admits weakness
steps: Say clearly that you are sorry and name what happened
Take responsibility for your part without excuses
Commit to a specific change
Follow through, and later show that you did
For bad circumstances you did not cause, a brief expression of regret can still signal care
situations: Apologizing to a client for a missed deadline
Making amends with a friend you hurt
Asking a stranger for a favor
Greeting a visitor who had a rough trip

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), material on apologies (a section named in the author's workbook); workbook exercise 'Apologize'; Greater Good summary of the book
source.underlying_research: Brooks, Dai and Schweitzer (2014), 'I'm Sorry About the Rain! Superfluous Apologies Demonstrate Empathic Concern and Increase Trust,' Social Psychological and Personality Science 5(4), 467-474 (four studies, including a field study at a train station). The physician-apology claim is reported from the book without a verified source.

insights.confidence_rationale: Apology advice confirmed in the workbook and the superfluous apology study confirmed as cited via Greater Good (abstract read: four studies, trust mediated by empathic concern). One paper from the author's team with no independent replication located; the sincere-apology steps are expert guidance.

insights.name: Find the layer where you differ
insights.explanation: Brooks describes conversation as a coordination game in which partners try to build shared understanding across several layers: content (what is said and how it sounds), emotions (how each person feels), beliefs (what each knows), motives (what each wants), and identity (who each person is). Difficult conversations usually involve a difference at one or more of these layers, and misunderstandings are more common than we think. When an exchange turns hard, asking which layer the gap is on helps you respond to the real issue instead of only the surface words.
insights.when_to_use: When a conversation suddenly turns tense or confusing, and when debriefing a difficult exchange afterward.
insights.worked_example: Two cofounders argue about whether to hire a salesperson. The surface is content (budget numbers), but one realizes the gap is at the motives layer (she wants growth, he wants runway) and partly identity (he sees himself as the careful one). Naming that shifts the talk from line items to how much risk each can accept.
common_mistakes: Arguing over content when the real difference is emotion, motive, or identity
Assuming shared understanding because no one objected
Treating an identity-level difference as a simple factual disagreement
steps: Notice the moment the conversation becomes hard
Ask which layer differs: content, emotions, beliefs, motives, or identity
Name or ask about that layer directly
Re-check shared understanding before moving on
situations: Debriefing an argument with a cofounder
Family disagreement that keeps recurring
A meeting where people seem to talk past each other

source.citation: Alison Wood Brooks, Talk: The Science of Conversation and the Art of Being Ourselves (Crown, 2025), opening framing of conversation as a coordination game and material on difficult moments; workbook exercises 'Coordination problems' and 'Sources of difficulty'
source.underlying_research: Author's synthesis; no single study. Related coordination findings the book cites include Mastroianni et al. (2021) on endings.

insights.confidence_rationale: Confirmed in the author's workbook as a framework from the book. It is a credible expert's diagnostic model rather than a tested intervention.
